hints: Focus on the difference between empirical and molecular formula, T could be $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}$ itself or a whole-number multiple of it.
Check the smallest possible molecule for each functional group, especially how many C atoms and O atoms a ketone and an ester must contain.
Ask yourself which groups can fit exactly one functional group into $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}$ or into $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}_2$ with no extra O atoms left over.
walkthrough:
**Understand what empirical formula means**

Remember, empirical means simplest ratio, not necessarily the true number of atoms. So T could be $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}$, or $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}_2$, or $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_3$, and so on.

$$\text{molecular formula} = n \times (\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O})$$

**Test aldehyde and ketone with one C=O group**

An aldehyde group is $-\text{CHO}$. Ethanal, $\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$, is exactly $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}$, so aldehyde is possible with n = 1.

A ketone group is $\text{C-CO-C}$ and needs at least 3 carbons. The smallest is propanone, $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}$, which does not match $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}$ or any multiple with only one O, so ketone is not possible.

**Test alcohol and ester by counting O atoms**

An alcohol with one $-\text{OH}$ and no other group has only one O. $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}$ as a saturated alcohol would be $\text{C}_2\text{H}_6\text{O}$, so $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}$ would need a C=C bond to give $\text{CH}_2=\text{CH-OH}$, an unstable enol that tautomerises. Cambridge does not count this as a stable alcohol.

An ester group is $-\text{COO-}$ and needs two O atoms. With n = 2, we get $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}_2$, which is exactly right for a saturated ester with one functional group, e.g. methyl propanoate or ethyl ethanoate. So ester is possible.

options.A: Incorrect. Alcohol (1) is not possible as a stable compound with only one functional group, the $\text{C}_2$ enol $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHOH}$ tautomerises to ethanal. Ester (3) alone is possible via $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}_2$, but pairing it with alcohol makes this option wrong.
options.B: Incorrect. Neither is possible with only one functional group. Alcohol (1) would require an unstable enol at $\text{C}_2$, and ketone (4) needs a minimum of 3 carbons like $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6\text{O}$, which cannot be made from multiples of $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}$ with a single O.
options.C: Correct. Aldehyde (2) fits n = 1 perfectly as ethanal, $\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$ ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}$). Ester (3) fits n = 2 perfectly as $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}_2$, which contains exactly the two O atoms needed for one $-\text{COO-}$ group, e.g. $\text{CH}_3\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$.
options.D: Incorrect. Aldehyde (2) alone is possible as ethanal, but ketone (4) is not. Students choosing this often remember both have C=O but forget a ketone needs two alkyl groups, so $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4\text{O}$ is too small and $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8\text{O}_2$ would leave a second O unaccounted for.
